[{"content": "[0] NOVATRANS LOGISTICS
[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com
[44] Data/IT: James Park, Senior Data Analyst -- james.park@novatrans-logistics.com
[47] We look forward to a productive engagement and anticipate that your analysis will provide the data-driven foundation needed to optimize our distribution network and strengthen our competitive position.
[49] Regards,
[51] David Chen
[52] Chief Operating Officer
[53] NovaTrans Logistics
[55] CONFIDENTIAL -- This memorandum and all accompanying data files are the property of NovaTrans Logistics and are intended solely for the use of the designated consulting team. Unauthorized distribution is prohibited.

    return p

def table(headers, rows, widths=None, font=8.5):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers)); t.style = 'Light Grid Accent 1'; t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    for i, x in enumerate(headers):
        c = t.rows[0].cells[i]; c.text = ''
        run = c.paragraphs[0].add_run(x); run.bold = True; run.font.size = Pt(font)
    for row in rows:
        cells = t.add_row().cells
        for i, x in enumerate(row):
            cells[i].text = ''
            run = cells[i].paragraphs[0].add_run(str(x)); run.font.size = Pt(font)
    if widths:
        for i, w in enumerate(widths):
            for row in t.rows: row.cells[i].width = Inches(w)
    return t

p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER

p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
para("Prepared by: Operations Consulting Team  |  For: Board of Directors, NovaTrans Logistics  |  Ref: COO Engagement Memo (D. Chen, 15 Jan 2024) + Board directive of the same cycle  |  Classification: Confidential", size=8.5, italic=True, space_after=8)

# ---------- 1. Methodology ----------
h("1. Methodology Statement", 1)
para("Board directive. Identify 3-5 of the 19 distribution plants as candidates for closure or consolidation using a composite scoring model, and operationalize 'structurally unviable' from the available data. We define a plant as structurally unviable when it exhibits one or more of: (i) stated daily capacity too small to absorb fixed operating overhead; (ii) per-unit warehousing cost materially above the network; (iii) a port role duplicated by other plants (redundant node); (iv) an unresolvable mismatch between stated capacity and observed workload; or (v) sustained service failure that consolidation would resolve.", space_after=6)
para("Scoring model. Each plant is scored 0-100 on five weighted factors; the weighted sum ranks consolidation candidacy (higher = stronger case):", space_after=4)
table(["Factor", "Wt", "Definition", "Rationale"],
 [("F1 Capacity-Scale Deficit", "25%", "Min-max inverted stated daily capacity (WhCapacities)", "Plants at 7-14 units/day stated capacity cannot absorb fixed overhead"),
  ("F2 Unit-Cost Disadvantage", "20%", "Min-max cost per unit (WhCosts)", "5.5x cost spread across network (0.371-2.036 $/unit)"),
  ("F3 Absorption Feasibility", "20%", "Port-sharing partners / max 6 (PlantPorts)", "Redundant port role = consolidatable; isolated port = transfer barrier"),
  ("F4 Throughput Evidence", "25%", "Log-scale inverted observed units/day (OrderList extract)", "Observed workload is the strongest viability evidence"),
  ("F5 Service & Customer Friction", "10%", "Late-shipment %, severity-weighted complaints, survey deficit", "Service failure raises transition risk and attrition exposure")],
 widths=[1.5, 0.5, 2.6, 2.4])
para("Data coverage and integrity. Structural factors (F1-F3, 65% of weight) draw on full-coverage reference files covering all 19 plants. Evidentiary factors (F4-F5, 35%) are observable only for the 7 plants present in the single-day order extract (9,215 orders dated 2013-05-26); the 12 uncovered plants receive a neutral score of 50 with an explicit flag - absence of evidence is not scored as evidence of zero throughput. The Data_Reconciliation tab of the accompanying workbook verifies the memo's claims: the ~2% late-shipment claim is confirmed at 2.08% (192 of 9,215), while the memo's 'PLANT01 handles ~1,070 units/day' and 'PLANT15 processes ~11 units/day' statements reproduce stated capacities from WhCapacities.csv exactly and conflate capacity with throughput; the claimed fixed-cost component of WhCosts is absent from the file. All figures in this brief are computed, not asserted.", space_after=8)

# ---------- 2. Consolidation Recommendation ----------
h("2. Consolidation Recommendation", 1)
para("Top-5 candidates by composite score (of 19 ranked; full ranking in the Composite_Score tab): PLANT19 (65.7), PLANT08 (64.7), PLANT09 (61.0), PLANT12 (60.2), PLANT18 (60.0). Watchlist (retain-and-monitor): PLANT11 (57.1), PLANT15 (54.9), PLANT16 (45.1).", space_after=4)
para("Redistribution plans and net cost impact. Port topology constrains absorption: a candidate's volume can only move to retained plants sharing at least one of its ports. Four of the five candidates sit in the PORT04 cluster (7 plants share one port), which is why consolidation is feasible there; PLANT18 (PORT11) and watchlist PLANT15 (PORT08) have no absorber at any price.", space_after=4)
rows = []
verdict_map = {"PLANT19":("Close","Redundant micro-node (capacity 7); no observed volume; 6 feasible absorbers","Role transfer to PORT04 cluster","$0 variable; savings = avoided fixed overhead"),
 "PLANT08":("Consolidate","Capacity 14 vs 277,008 observed units/day; late rate 17.65% (network worst)","All volume to PLANT13 (PORT04)","-$14,723/day (-$5.37M annualized)"),
 "PLANT09":("Consolidate","Capacity 11 vs 223,830 units/day; lowest satisfaction (2.50/5), 50% recommend","All volume to PLANT13 (PORT04)","+$1,038/day variable, offset by fixed-cost avoidance"),
 "PLANT12":("Consolidate","Cost/unit 0.773 vs network median ~0.53; 2 escalated wrong-item complaints","All volume to PLANT13 (PORT04)","-$33,984/day (-$12.40M annualized)"),
 "PLANT18":("Close (conditional)","Highest unit cost (2.036 $/unit) but unique PORT11 access - no absorber","Port-access transfer or 3PL at PORT11 first","$0 observed; +24.9% carrier-matched rate premium if PORT11 volume rerouted via PORT04")}

table(["Candidate","Score","Action","Structural Evidence","Redistribution Plan","Net Cost Impact"],
 rows, widths=[0.8, 0.5, 0.9, 2.1, 1.5, 1.5])
para("Combined program. Closing PLANT19 and PLANT18 and consolidating PLANT08, PLANT09 and PLANT12 into PLANT13 (primary absorber, cheapest retained CPU at 0.470 $/unit) shrinks the PORT04 cluster from 7 plants to 4. Fixed-cost avoidance of $150k-$400k per closed node (parameterized - not in client data) adds $0.75M-$2.0M per year at full wind-down. Capacity headroom check in capacity-equivalent units (conversion 5,096.4 observed units per stated capacity unit) is directional only pending an ERP unit-basis audit.", space_after=8)

# ---------- 3. Risk ----------
h("3. Implementation Risk Assessment", 1)
para("Customer attrition risk (Q4-2023 complaint log and satisfaction survey, cross-referenced in the Risk_Matrix tab). All three consolidation candidates with VOC coverage rate High risk:", space_after=4)
table(["Candidate","Evidence","Exposure","Mitigation"],
 [("PLANT09","Satisfaction 2.50/5 (network low), 50% would recommend, 3 complaints (2 open, incl. High-severity C-014 adjacent-bin pick error)","Only 2 order customers - each loss material","White-glove migration; close C-009 (22 days open) and C-014 pre-move"),
  ("PLANT08","Late-shipment rate 17.65% (network worst); 2 of 3 complaints open incl. carrier-capacity-driven C-002 (22 days)","5 order customers","Notify accounts 30 days ahead; copy complaint history to PLANT13; weekly late% monitor"),
  ("PLANT12","2 escalated wrong-item complaints open 13-19 days (labeling mix-ups at high-volume shifts)","13 order customers - highest exposure among candidates","Migrate in 3 waves; transfer bin-labeling audit to PLANT13; 90-day complaint watch")],
 widths=[0.8, 2.9, 1.6, 1.7])
para("Structural and data risks. (1) PLANT18 closure strands PORT11: no other plant holds that access; the carrier-matched rate premium for rerouting via PORT04 is +24.9% (V444_8) with identical transit time, so the precondition is a contracting exercise - transfer or 3PL before closure. (2) Watchlist PLANT15 (PORT08) has no carrier overlap with PORT04 rate cards: any closure would reprice its lane from an unquantified base - monitor, do not close. (3) The order extract is one day and covers 7 of 19 plants; VOC data is ten years newer (2023 vs 2013); unit bases differ by ~5,096x. Phase 1 of any program must be a full-period, all-plant extract plus ERP unit-basis audit before physical moves. (4) PLANT19 and PLANT18 have no survey or complaint coverage: run a targeted VOC pulse (target >= 60% response) before executing either closure.", space_after=8)

h("4. Go/No-Go Matrix", 1)
table(["Candidate","Recommended Action","Confidence","Binding Condition","First 90 Days"],
 [("PLANT19","Close","High","None (redundant node, 6 absorbers)","Transfer PORT04 service role; wind down site"),
  ("PLANT08","Consolidate","High","PLANT13 capacity intake confirmed","Move volume in 2 waves; resolve open complaints first"),
  ("PLANT09","Consolidate","Medium","Retention plan for 2 named accounts accepted","White-glove cutover; close C-009/C-014"),
  ("PLANT12","Consolidate","Medium","3-wave customer migration plan signed off","Wave 1 (5 accounts); labeling audit at PLANT13"),

 widths=[0.8, 1.2, 0.8, 2.0, 2.2])
para("Retain-and-monitor (no action this cycle): PLANT11 (57.1 - redundant but retains option value as absorber), PLANT15 (54.9 - unabsorbable port), PLANT16 (45.1 - costly but load-bearing and port-unique). Re-score after the phase-1 data refresh.", space_after=8)

table(["Dimension","COO Memo (Jan 15, 2024)","Board Directive","Consultant Position"],

para("Full quantitative support: NovaTrans_Plant_Consolidation_Scoring_Model.xlsx (Composite_Score, Consolidation_Scenarios, Risk_Matrix, Data_Reconciliation tabs).", size=8.5, italic=True)

1. Purpose & Methodology Statement (~1 page):
- Board directive: 3–5 candidates for closure/consolidation; "structurally unviable" operationalized.
- Definition: A plant is structurally unviable when (a) stated capacity too small to absorb fixed overhead, (b) unit cost materially above network, (c) its port role duplicated elsewhere, (d) no observed throughput / cannot support observed load, (e) service failures.
- Model: 5 weighted factors, weights + rationale table (compact), data coverage statement (7/19 transactional, neutral scoring for rest, single-day extract caveat).

2. Consolidation Recommendation (~1.5 pages):
- Results: top-5 with scores (small table), then per-candidate metrics + redistribution plan (table with 5 rows: candidate, verdict, volume, absorber, $ impact, precondition).

3. Implementation Risk Assessment (~1 page):
- Customer risk: PLANT09 (sat 2.50, 50% recommend, 2 customers), PLANT08 (17.65% late, 2 open complaints), PLANT12 (13 customers, 2 escalated complaints open 13–19 days). 15/15 complaint customers have survey responses; order customers not linkable.
- Operational: unit-basis mismatch (5,096×), fixed costs unknown, PORT11 access transfer for PLANT18, no absorber for PORT08.
- Data risk: extract is 1 day in 2013; VOC 2023.

4. Go/No-Go Matrix (table): Candidate | Action | Confidence | Key condition | First 90 days.

5. Memo vs Board alignment (~0.5 page):
- Align: warehouse utilization concern (memo §2) ↔ board consolidation directive; late-shipment root-cause scope explains PLANT08; both want data-driven recommendations.
- Conflict: memo asks for network-wide efficiency review incl. freight-cost savings and capacity rebalancing with 10-page exec report; board directive narrows to structural consolidation. [5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com

[{"content": "[0] NOVATRANS LOGISTICS
[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.
[40] 7. Points of Contact
[41] For any questions regarding data interpretation, system access, or scope clarifications, please direct inquiries to:
[42] Primary: David Chen, COO -- david.chen@novatrans-logistics.com
[43] Secondary: Maria Santos, Director of Operations -- maria.santos@novatrans-logistics.com
[44] Data/IT: James Park, Senior Data Analyst -- james.park@novatrans-logistics.com
[47] We look forward to a productive engagement and anticipate that your analysis will provide the data-driven foundation needed to optimize our distribution network and strengthen our competitive position.
[49] Regards,
[51] David Chen
[52] Chief Operating Officer
[53] NovaTrans Logistics
[55] CONFIDENTIAL -- This memorandum and all accompanying data files are the property of NovaTrans Logistics and are intended solely for the use of the designated consulting team. Unauthorized distribution is prohibited.

[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.

[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.

NovaTrans operates 19 distribution plants, and the board is concerned that some may be structurally unviable. The COO's memo does not define this term — you must operationalize it using the available data.

Your first deliverable is a Plant Consolidation Scoring Model (Excel workbook, .xlsx) with four tabs. The \"Composite_Score\" tab should rank all 19 plants on consolidation candidacy using a weighted model with documented weighting rationale. The \"Consolidation_Scenarios\" tab should model volume redistribution for your top closure candidates, accounting for network topology constraints — port access determines which plants can absorb volume from others — and calculating net cost impact. [10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.
[37] 6. Timeline & Presentation
[38] The deadline for submission of all deliverables is two (2) weeks from the date of this memorandum. Upon submission, the consulting team will be invited to present findings and recommendations to the NovaTrans executive leadership team, including the CEO, CFO, VP of Operations, and VP of Supply Chain.
[39] Please allocate approximately 45 minutes for the presentation, followed by a 15-minute Q&A session. Presentation materials may be prepared in addition to the deliverables listed above, at your discretion.

- 19 plants; capacities range 7 (PLANT19) to 1070 (PLANT01). Note PLANT09 capacity is 11 — same as PLANT15 (both 11; that's why 18 unique values).
- Wait, there's a data inconsistency: PLANT09 handled 223,830 units in one day with capacity of 11 units/day?? That's utilization of 20,348×. And PLANT08 capacity 14 but processed 277,008 units. And PLANT03 capacity 1013 vs 28.6M units. So "Daily_Capacity" is clearly NOT in the same units as Unit_Quant — this is a known quirk of the SCLP dataset (from the Brunel University London "Supply Chain Logistics Problem" dataset, WhCapacities is in a different unit). The memo says "PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day" and "PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day" — those match WhCapacities values exactly. So the memo's throughput claims = stated capacity figures. The observed throughput from the order extract is in a different unit scale (millions of units). This is a reconciliation finding: units are inconsistent between OrderList (Unit_Quant) and WhCapacities (Daily_Capacity); utilization ratio observed/capacity is not meaningful at face value; must normalize.

How to handle utilization honestly: compute observed units/day ÷ stated capacity, but note unit mismatch → ratio is astronomically >1 for covered plants, which is implausible as physical units. Options: treat WhCapacities as relative scale index. For scoring, better to use within-source percentiles rather than raw ratios:
- Throughput Index (for covered plants): rank on observed units/day.
- For uncovered plants: no observed volume → structural candidates.
- Capacity-scale Index: rank on Daily_Capacity (structural scale, relative within source).

Your engagement brief is in \"COO_Engagement_Memo.docx,\" but the board has added a new directive — identify 3–5 candidate plants for closure or consolidation based on a composite scoring model you must design. The COO's memo does not define this term — you must operationalize it using the available data.

Your first deliverable is a Plant Consolidation Scoring Model (Excel workbook, .xlsx) with four tabs. The \"Composite_Score\" tab should rank all 19 plants on consolidation candidacy using a weighted model with documented weighting rationale. The \"Consolidation_Scenarios\" tab should model volume redistribution for your top closure candidates, accounting for network topology constraints — port access determines which plants can absorb volume from others — and calculating net cost impact. [{"content": "[0] NOVATRANS LOGISTICS
[1] Delivering Excellence Across Every Mile
[3] INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
[5] DATE:  January 15, 2024
[6] TO:  Operations Consulting Team
[7] FROM:  David Chen, Chief Operating Officer, NovaTrans Logistics
[8] SUBJECT:  Engagement Brief: Distribution Network Efficiency Review
[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.
[27] Assess warehouse capacity utilization across all 19 plants. Determine which facilities are over- or under-utilized relative to their stated capacity and recommend rebalancing strategies.
[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.
[30] 4. Available Data
[31] The following data exports and reference materials are provided for your analysis. Source files may reflect different operating periods unless otherwise noted:
[33] 5. Expected Deliverables
[34] Upon completion of the engagement, we expect the following deliverables:
[35] Excel-Based Analysis Workbook. A comprehensive workbook containing separate tabs for each analytical dimension (freight cost analysis, warehouse utilization, late shipment analysis, carrier/route comparison, etc.). Each tab should include source data summaries, pivot analyses, charts where appropriate, and key findings highlighted in a consistent format.
[36] Executive Summary Report (Word Document). A standalone Word document (maximum 10 pages) summarizing the engagement findings, key insights, and prioritized recommendations. This document will be circulated to the executive leadership team and should be written at a level appropriate for a C-suite audience. Include an executive summary on the first page, followed by detailed sections for each analytical area, and conclude with a prioritized action plan.

And PLANT03 capacity 1013 vs 28.6M units. So "Daily_Capacity" is clearly NOT in the same units as Unit_Quant — this is a known quirk of the SCLP dataset (from the Brunel University London "Supply Chain Logistics Problem" dataset, WhCapacities is in a different unit). The memo says "PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day" and "PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day" — those match WhCapacities values exactly. So the memo's throughput claims = stated capacity figures. The observed throughput from the order extract is in a different unit scale (millions of units). This is a reconciliation finding: units are inconsistent between OrderList (Unit_Quant) and WhCapacities (Daily_Capacity); utilization ratio observed/capacity is not meaningful at face value; must normalize.

How to handle utilization honestly: compute observed units/day ÷ stated capacity, but note unit mismatch → ratio is astronomically >1 for covered plants, which is implausible as physical units. Options: treat WhCapacities as relative scale index. For scoring, better to use within-source percentiles rather than raw ratios:
- Throughput Index (for covered plants): rank on observed units/day.
- For uncovered plants: no observed volume → structural candidates.
- Capacity-scale Index: rank on Daily_Capacity (structural scale, relative within source).

Also PLANT09/PLANT08 have tiny capacities (11, 14) but big observed volume — those are *over*-utilized relative to stated capacity (interesting: the tiny-capacity plants that DO have volume might need capacity relief, while similar-capacity plants with no observed volume are redundancy). PLANT19 capacity 7, port PORT04 shared with 6 others, no orders, cost 0.64. PLANT17 cap 8, unique PORT10, no orders, cost 0.43. PLANT15 cap 11, unique PORT08, no orders, cost 1.415 (2nd highest!). Consolidation topology logic: A plant can absorb volume from another only if they share a port (port access determines absorption). So for a candidate with a unique port (e.g., PLANT15 → PORT08), NO other plant can absorb its volume because no other plant has PORT08 access. Hmm — but wait, can absorbing plants actually *ship from* the candidate's port? The constraint says port access determines which plants can absorb volume from others. If a candidate's port is unique to it, closing it means losing that port's service → volume can't be absorbed without port expansion → scenario = "no feasible absorber; require port access transfer" — that's a legitimate scenario output: cost of establishing access vs. closure savings. Alternatively, the absorb direction: plants that share ANY port can absorb. For PORT04 cluster candidates (PLANT19 cap 7!), 6 absorbers available.

Rationale: throughput is the strongest direct evidence of viability; absence of any orders in a full-day network extract is the strongest structural signal.

[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.

[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.

[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. [12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.

[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.

- 19 plants; capacities range 7 (PLANT19) to 1070 (PLANT01). Note PLANT09 capacity is 11 — same as PLANT15 (both 11; that's why 18 unique values).
- Wait, there's a data inconsistency: PLANT09 handled 223,830 units in one day with capacity of 11 units/day?? That's utilization of 20,348×. And PLANT08 capacity 14 but processed 277,008 units. And PLANT03 capacity 1013 vs 28.6M units. So "Daily_Capacity" is clearly NOT in the same units as Unit_Quant — this is a known quirk of the SCLP dataset (from the Brunel University London "Supply Chain Logistics Problem" dataset, WhCapacities is in a different unit). The memo says "PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day" and "PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day" — those match WhCapacities values exactly. So the memo's throughput claims = stated capacity figures. The observed throughput from the order extract is in a different unit scale (millions of units). This is a reconciliation finding: units are inconsistent between OrderList (Unit_Quant) and WhCapacities (Daily_Capacity); utilization ratio observed/capacity is not meaningful at face value; must normalize.

How to handle utilization honestly: compute observed units/day ÷ stated capacity, but note unit mismatch → ratio is astronomically >1 for covered plants, which is implausible as physical units. Options: treat WhCapacities as relative scale index. For scoring, better to use within-source percentiles rather than raw ratios:
- Throughput Index (for covered plants): rank on observed units/day.
- For uncovered plants: no observed volume → structural candidates.
- Capacity-scale Index: rank on Daily_Capacity (structural scale, relative within source).

Also PLANT09/PLANT08 have tiny capacities (11, 14) but big observed volume — those are *over*-utilized relative to stated capacity (interesting: the tiny-capacity plants that DO have volume might need capacity relief, while similar-capacity plants with no observed volume are redundancy). PLANT19 capacity 7, port PORT04 shared with 6 others, no orders, cost 0.64. PLANT17 cap 8, unique PORT10, no orders, cost 0.43. PLANT15 cap 11, unique PORT08, no orders, cost 1.415 (2nd highest!). PLANT18 cap 111, unique PORT11, no orders, cost 2.036 (highest!). PLANT16 cap 457, unique PORT09, has orders (173, 245k units), cost 1.92 (2nd highest) → high cost + high volume.

Topology: PORT04 cluster = PLANT03, 08, 09, 11, 12, 13, 19 (7 plants) — massive redundancy at PORT04. PORT01/PORT02 cluster = PLANT01, 07, 10. Isolated-port plants: PLANT02 (PORT03), PLANT04 (PORT05), PLANT14 (PORT07), PLANT15 (PORT08), PLANT16 (PORT09), PLANT17 (PORT10), PLANT18 (PORT11), PLANT05/PLANT06 (PORT06 pair).

Consolidation topology logic: A plant can absorb volume from another only if they share a port (port access determines absorption). So for a candidate with a unique port (e.g., PLANT15 → PORT08), NO other plant can absorb its volume because no other plant has PORT08 access. Hmm — but wait, can absorbing plants actually *ship from* the candidate's port? The constraint says port access determines which plants can absorb volume from others. If a candidate's port is unique to it, closing it means losing that port's service → volume can't be absorbed without port expansion → scenario = "no feasible absorber; require port access transfer" — that's a legitimate scenario output: cost of establishing access vs. closure savings. Alternatively, the absorb direction: plants that share ANY port can absorb. For PORT04 cluster candidates (PLANT19 cap 7!), 6 absorbers available.

Now, which plants are top closure candidates? Let me design the composite score:

Factors (weighted, all scaled 0–100, higher = stronger consolidation candidacy):

F1 Scale/Capacity Index (20%): Daily_Capacity percentile (min-max normalized, inverted: small capacity → high score). Rationale: plants with stated capacity ≤ ~15 units/day cannot economically absorb fixed operating overheads; scale is the primary structural viability driver. Source: WhCapacities (full 19-plant coverage).

F2 Observed Throughput/Utilization (25%): For the 7 plants with order data: observed units/day vs stated capacity. Because of unit mismatch, compute utilization ratio = observed/capacity; then normalize within the covered subset. Over-utilized plants = NOT closure candidates (they're load-bearing); under-observed = candidates. For the 12 uncovered plants: zero observed throughput → score 100 (max candidacy) with data caveat. Rationale: throughput is the strongest direct evidence of viability; absence of any orders in a full-day network extract is the strongest structural signal.

Hmm wait — but that conflates "no data coverage" with "no throughput". The 12 uncovered plants include the 3 origin ports issue: the extract only covers shipments originating at PORT04/05/09. Plants at other ports simply can't appear. This is a serious caveat. But the board asked to rank 19 plants on available data; I must document the coverage limitation and handle it honestly. Design choice: F2 = "Transactional Throughput Evidence": observed units/day percentile for covered; for uncovered, score = neutral 50 with flag? Hmm, but then PLANT15/17/18 (no orders, tiny capacity, high cost) would rank below covered over-utilized plants... Actually let me reconsider.

Alternative cleaner design: split the score into "structural" factors (full 19 coverage: scale, cost, topology redundancy) and "evidentiary" factors (only 7 coverage: throughput, service). Weight structural factors higher (65%) so all 19 plants can be ranked fairly, and apply a documented treatment for missing evidentiary data:
- F1 Capacity Scale (25%) — structural, all 19
- F2 Unit Cost Disadvantage (20%) — structural, all 19 (Cost_Per_Unit percentile; higher cost → higher candidacy)
- F3 Topology Redundancy (20%) — structural, all 19: whether plant's port function is duplicated by other plants (shared ports → redundant; isolated → hard to consolidate)
- F4 Throughput Deficit (20%) — evidentiary: observed daily units vs stated capacity band; uncovered plants scored at "no evidence of throughput" → moderately high (75) with flag, covered plants scored on utilization percentile
- F5 Service Risk / Customer Friction (15%) — evidentiary: complaints + late% + survey; uncovered → neutral 50 flagged

2. High unit cost — PLANT18 (2.04), PLANT16 (1.92), PLANT15 (1.42) vs network median ~0.53

PLANT16 (cost 1.92, cap 457, volume, isolated port) — costly but load-bearing and unique port → Retain-and-Monitor or consolidation of cost structure. PLANT11 (cap 332, no orders, PORT04 cluster, cost 0.555) — redundant. PLANT12 (cap 209, has 300 orders/112k units, PORT04 cluster, cost 0.773, 2 escalated complaints). PLANT05/PLANT06 (PORT06 pair, no orders, caps 385/49) — PLANT06 tiny + shares port with PLANT05 → consolidatable pair.

[10] 1. Background & Context
[11] NovaTrans Logistics is a mid-sized, port-based logistics company specializing in freight distribution and supply chain fulfillment. We currently operate 19 distribution plants strategically positioned across our network, handling the movement of goods between manufacturing origins, inland warehouses, and port terminals.
[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. Our Q4 2023 customer satisfaction survey data reinforces this concern.
[21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. This imbalance raises questions about capacity allocation, fixed cost absorption, and whether certain low-volume plants should be consolidated or repurposed.
[22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. Some carriers may deliver comparable service levels at materially lower rates on specific lanes, but we lack a consolidated view to validate this hypothesis and act on it.
[23] 3. Scope of Engagement
[24] We are engaging your team to conduct a comprehensive review of our distribution network operations. Specifically, we request that you:
[25] Analyze the order and shipment data to identify operational bottlenecks, including transit-time outliers, mode-selection inefficiencies, and demand concentration patterns.
[26] Evaluate freight cost efficiency across carriers, transportation modes, and specific origin-destination routes. Identify lanes where cost savings are achievable without degrading service quality.

[28] Identify root causes of late shipments. Correlate late-shipment data with plant origin, carrier assignment, service level, and transportation mode to isolate the primary drivers of delays.
[29] Provide actionable recommendations supported by data. Each recommendation should include an estimated impact (cost savings, service improvement, or capacity optimization) and an implementation priority ranking.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, json
def nat(x):
    if isinstance(x,(np.integer,)): return int(x)

    raise TypeError(str(type(x)))
pd.set_option("display.width", 250); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)

pp = pd.read_csv('task_folder/PlantPorts.csv')
xl = pd.ExcelFile('task_folder/Customer_Satisfaction_Survey_Q4.xlsx')
sur, com = xl.parse('Survey_Results'), xl.parse('Complaint_Log')
fact = pd.read_csv('.scratch/fact_scored.csv', index_col=0)
plants = sorted(cap.Plant_Code.unique())
capl = cap.set_index('Plant_Code')['Daily_Capacity']; cst = cost.set_index('Plant_Code')['Cost_Per_Unit']
ports = pp.groupby('Plant_Code')['Ports'].apply(lambda s: sorted(s)).to_dict()
partners = {p: [q for q in plants if q!=p and set(ports[p])&set(ports[q])] for p in plants}
scale = o.Unit_Quant.sum()/capl.sum()
cands = list(fact.index[:5]); retained = [p for p in plants if p not in cands]

scen_rows=[]
for cand in cands:
    absorbers = [q for q in partners[cand] if q in retained]
    abs_detail=[{'plant':q,'cpu':round(cst[q],6),'cap':int(capl[q]),
                 'spare_cap_units':round(capl[q]-(fact.loc[q,'units']/scale if fact.loc[q,'covered'] else 0),1)} for q in sorted(absorbers,key=lambda x:cst[x])]
    vol = float(fact.loc[cand,'units']) if fact.loc[cand,'covered'] else 0.0
    alloc, remaining, wl = [], vol, 0.0
    for a in sorted(absorbers,key=lambda x:cst[x]):
        if remaining<=1e-9: break
        spare_u = (capl[a]-fact.loc[a,'units']/scale)*scale if fact.loc[a,'covered'] else capl[a]*scale
        take = min(remaining, max(spare_u,0))
        if take<=0: continue
        d = cst[a]-cst[cand]; wl += take*d
        alloc.append({'to':a,'units':int(round(take)),'cpu_from':round(cst[cand],6),'cpu_to':round(cst[a],6),
                      'delta_per_unit':round(d,6),'delta_per_day':round(take*d,2),'delta_per_yr':round(take*d*365,2)})
        remaining -= take
    scen_rows.append({'cand':cand,'score':round(float(fact.loc[cand,'composite']),1),'cap':int(capl[cand]),
        'cpu':round(float(cst[cand]),6),'vol_obs':int(vol),
        'orders':int(fact.loc[cand,'orders']) if fact.loc[cand,'covered'] else 0,
        'cust':int(fact.loc[cand,'cust']) if fact.loc[cand,'covered'] else 0,
        'ports':ports[cand],'n_abs':len(absorbers),'absorbers':abs_detail,'alloc':alloc,
        'vol_unalloc':int(remaining),'wl_delta_day':round(float(wl),2),'wl_delta_yr':round(float(wl*365),2),
        'late_pct':round(float(fact.loc[cand,'late_pct']),2) if fact.loc[cand,'covered'] else None})
json.dump(scen_rows, open('.scratch/scenarios.json','w'), indent=1, default=nat)
for r in scen_rows:
    print(r['cand'], "score",r['score'],"cap",r['cap'],"vol",r['vol_obs'],"abs",[a['plant'] for a in r['absorbers']],
          "alloc",[(a['to'],a['units']) for a in r['alloc']],"unalloc",r['vol_unalloc'],"WL/day",r['wl_delta_day'],"WL/yr",r['wl_delta_yr'])

fr = pd.read_csv('task_folder/references/FreightRates.csv'); fr.columns=[c.strip() for c in fr.columns]; fr['Mode_DSC']=fr['Mode_DSC'].str.strip()
prem=[]
for orig, ref in [('PORT11','PORT04'),('PORT08','PORT04'),('PORT10','PORT04')]:
    for carr in sorted(fr.Carrier.unique()):
        a = fr[(fr.Orig_Port==orig)&(fr.Carrier==carr)&(fr.Dest_Port=='PORT09')]
        b = fr[(fr.Orig_Port==ref)&(fr.Carrier==carr)&(fr.Dest_Port=='PORT09')]
        if len(a) and len(b):
            prem.append({'stranded':orig,'ref':ref,'carrier':carr,'rate_stranded':round(a.Rate.mean(),4),
                'rate_ref':round(b.Rate.mean(),4),'premium_pct':round((a.Rate.mean()/b.Rate.mean()-1)*100,1),
                'mincost_stranded':round(a.Min_Cost.mean(),2),'mincost_ref':round(b.Min_Cost.mean(),2),
                'tpt_stranded':round(a.TPT_Day_Count.mean(),1),'tpt_ref':round(b.TPT_Day_Count.mean(),1),
                'mode':a.Mode_DSC.mode().iloc[0]})
pm = pd.DataFrame(prem); pm.to_csv('.scratch/stranded_premium.csv', index=False)
print("\nStranded-lane premiums:\n", pm.to_string())

late_max = fact.loc[fact.covered,'late_pct'].max(); sev_max = fact.loc[fact.covered,'sev_w'].max()
risk=[]
for cand in cands:
    row = fact.loc[cand]
    if bool(row.covered):
        comp_c = row.sev_w/sev_max*100 if row.sev_w>0 else 0
        sat_c = 0.5*((5-row.sat)/4*100)+0.5*(100-row.rec_pct)
        idx = 0.35*comp_c + 0.25*(row.open_n/row.comp_n*100 if row.comp_n>0 else 0) + 0.40*sat_c
        rating = 'High' if idx>=55 else ('Medium' if idx>=30 else 'Low')
        comp_custs = sorted(com[com.Plant_Code==cand].Customer_ID.unique())
        risk.append({'plant':cand,'orders':int(row.orders),'cust':int(row.cust),'late_pct':round(row.late_pct,2),
            'comp_n':int(row.comp_n),'sev_w':int(row.sev_w),'open_n':int(row.open_n),'days':round(row.days,1),
            'survey_n':int(row.n),'sat':round(row.sat,2),'rec_pct':round(row.rec_pct,1),
            'risk_idx':round(float(idx),1),'rating':rating,'compl_custs':len(comp_custs),
            'linked':len(set(comp_custs)&set(sur.Customer_ID))})
    else:
        risk.append({'plant':cand,'orders':0,'cust':0,'late_pct':None,'comp_n':0,'sev_w':0,'open_n':0,'days':None,
            'survey_n':0,'sat':None,'rec_pct':None,'risk_idx':None,'rating':'Not assessable','compl_custs':0,'linked':0})
rk = pd.DataFrame(risk); rk.to_csv('.scratch/risk.csv', index=False)
print("\nRISK:\n", rk.to_string())
json.dump({'scale':round(scale,1),'cands':cands,'late_max':float(late_max),'sev_max':float(sev_max),
           'tot_cap':int(capl.sum()),'tot_units':int(o.Unit_Quant.sum()),
           'late_n':int((o.Ship_Late_Day_Count>0).sum()),'n_orders':int(len(o))}, open('.scratch/params.json','w'), default=nat)
print("\nScale factor:", round(scale,1))

[12] On an annual basis, our network processes roughly 9,000+ individual shipments spanning multiple transportation modes, including SEA, AIR, and ROAD. We serve a diverse portfolio of customers under three distinct service levels:
[13] CRF (Cross-dock Freight) -- Goods are consolidated at a cross-dock facility and forwarded without long-term storage, optimizing transit speed.
[14] DTD (Door-to-Door) -- Full end-to-end delivery from origin to the customer's designated receiving location.
[15] DTP (Door-to-Port) -- Delivery from the origin point to the designated port terminal, where the customer or a third-party forwarder assumes custody.
[16] Our ERP system captures detailed transactional data for every order, including origin/destination plant codes, shipment dates, carrier assignments, freight costs, and warehouse throughput metrics. This data forms the foundation for the analysis we are requesting.
[17] 2. Problem Statement
[18] Despite steady revenue growth over the past three fiscal years, our operating margins have come under increasing pressure. Preliminary internal reviews point to several areas of concern that require rigorous, data-driven investigation:
[19] Rising Freight Costs. Overall freight expenditure has increased disproportionately relative to shipment volume. The AIR transportation mode, in particular, exhibits significantly higher per-unit costs compared to SEA and ROAD, yet continues to be utilized for shipments where alternative modes may be viable. We need a clear understanding of cost drivers across carriers and routes.
[20] Late Shipments & Customer Dissatisfaction. Approximately 2% of all orders ship late relative to their scheduled ship date. While this figure may appear modest, it translates to a meaningful number of affected customers each quarter, eroding satisfaction and jeopardizing key accounts. [21] Uneven Warehouse Utilization. Warehouse throughput varies dramatically across our plant network. For example, PLANT01 handles approximately 1,070 units per day, making it one of our highest-volume facilities, while PLANT15 processes only around 11 units per day. [22] Carrier & Route Cost Variability. We suspect that significant cost-efficiency differences exist between carrier-route combinations. [23] 3. Scope of Engagement
